tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the peer-reviewed TVLSI 2016 paper is checked into the repo (docs/He_TVLSI_15.pdf) and its abstract and Section IV state 19.56x over KLU 1.2.0 and 47.13x over UMFPACK 5.6.2 on UFL circuit matrices (numeric factorization only, K40 GPU, 2x Xeon E5-2670 host, CUDA 5.0). Not A: compiler flags are not stated, the baseline harness is not public, and the paper measured GLU 1.0, not the GLU3.0 code now in the repo.

corrections.claimed_speedup: TVLSI 2016 (GLU 1.0): on typical UFL circuit matrices about 19.56x over KLU and 47.13x over UMFPACK (also 5.71x / 1.46x over single- / 16-threaded PARDISO and 1.47x over a GPU left-looking solver); on general UFL matrices 39.39x over KLU and 24.04x over UMFPACK (geometric mean). Times are numeric factorization only, excluding preprocessing and symbolic analysis. GLU3.0 (IEEE D&T 2020, docs/Peng_DT_2020.pdf Table I): 3.51x arithmetic / 2.81x geometric mean over 32-thread NICSLU on 15 circuit matrices, numeric factorization time.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: TVLSI 2016: CUDA 5.0, compiler flags not stated; GLU3.0 paper: C++ and CUDA C compiled with -O3
corrections.hardware: TVLSI 2016: NVIDIA Tesla K40 (all GPU results), host with two 8-core Xeon E5-2670 and 64 GB DDR3-1600; GLU3.0 paper: NVIDIA GTX TITAN X (Maxwell) with Xeon E5-2698 v3 and 128 GB
corrections.workload: Sparse LU numeric factorization of circuit-simulation and general matrices from the University of Florida (SuiteSparse) collection plus self-generated RLC mesh networks, GPU versus CPU direct solvers (KLU 1.2.0, UMFPACK 5.6.2, PARDISO 5.0.0); preprocessing and symbolic analysis excluded from timings.
corrections.caveats: The 19.56x / 47.13x figures are from the TVLSI 2016 GLU 1.0 paper (docs/He_TVLSI_15.pdf); baselines are old (KLU 1.2.0, UMFPACK 5.6.2, PARDISO 5.0.0) and timings cover numeric factorization only, so symbolic analysis and preprocessing (where KLU is cheap) are excluded. GLU is slower than the CPU solvers on very small circuits (circuit_2, rajat15), and on the self-generated RLC meshes 16-threaded PARDISO is the best CPU solver. The repo now holds GLU3.0, which the 2020 paper measured in single precision against 32-thread NICSLU (2.81x geometric mean); pyglu also runs float32 on the GPU, so precision differs from the double-precision CPU baselines. Recent commits (Feb 2026) fixed a CUDA __syncthreads() deadlock on a divergent path and unchecked CUDA calls, so published numbers were measured on code with those issues. The repo bundles NICSLU (src/nicslu) under LGPL-2.1-or-later alongside the BSD-3-Clause GLU code. README has no benchmark numbers.

notes: Found the TVLSI 2016 and GLU3.0 (D&T 2020) papers as PDFs in docs/ and confirmed the numbers there. Metadata: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt), 47 stars, 12 forks, last commit 2026-07-04 on master, so active.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the work is peer reviewed (IEEE Access vol. 10, 2022, pp. 85960-85974, per the README bibtex) and a search result quoting its abstract gives up to 27.8x, 1.81x and 2.04x over cuSPARSE, nsparse and spECK on 26 matrices on a Tesla V100. B rests on venue plus abstract per earlier precedents; the paper (arxiv, ieeexplore, hkust pages) is blocked here. The repo has the harness (OpSparse/src/reg_opsparse.cu, reg_cusparse.cu; nvcc -O3 -arch=compute_70 -code=sm_70) but no host CPU model, so not A.

corrections.workload: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM, C = A*A) on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 over 26 commonly used matrices (paper abstract per search result); the repo harness downloads webbase-1M and has reg_opsparse, reg_cusparse, nsparse and spECK drivers.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the abstract of the IEEE Access 2022 paper (arXiv 2206.07244) as quoted in search results; the paper itself was not opened (arxiv, ieeexplore and hkust.edu.hk hosts are egress-blocked). The 'up to' figures (27.8x, 1.81x, 2.04x) were confirmed by this verifier's search; the averages (7.35x, 1.43x, 1.52x) come from the search agent's snippet. A later third-party study ('Optimizing General Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on the GPU', ACM) reports average speedups over cuSPARSE of 4.91x for OpSparse versus 5.67x for spECK and 3.47x for TileSpGEMM, so the authors' figure is on the favourable end and spECK can be faster in other matrix sets. Single-GPU (V100, CUDA 11.2) results; host CPU not stated. The repo bundles nsparse and spECK copies for the comparison; the single MIT LICENSE lists their copyright holders (Tokyo Institute of Technology, Mathias Parger), and cuSPARSE is only called through its API. Last commit 2022.

notes: Usability corrected to copyable: the top-level MIT LICENSE covers OpSparse and the bundled nsparse/spECK sources, and the cuSPARSE harness only calls the library. Metadata: 16 stars, 4 forks, 9 commits, last commit 2022-08-23 (abandoned). benchmark_url set to the arXiv preprint of the IEEE Access paper (not opened; blocked).
